data.title: Zemianske Podhradie – Martákova skala, a hillfort in the White Carpathians
data.excerpt: Martákova skala above the Bošáca valley was fortified by the people of the Lusatian culture, and the position was later used by Celts, by the Germanic Quadi and, in the 9th to 11th centuries, by the Slavs. J. Ľ. Holuby dug here in 1887; a Celtic hoard of iron tools and a Slavic belt loop from a sword belt show how long this place mattered.
data.metaDescription: A hillfort above the Bošáca valley with a Lusatian rampart in three phases, a Celtic hoard of iron tools and Slavic finds from a sword belt and harness.

children.text: The area of the White Carpathians was settled by man as early as the Stone Age, because it is a territory with deposits of raw material suitable for making chipped stone tools. Later – in the Late and Final Bronze Age and on into the Hallstatt period (1,200 – 700 – 500 years BC) – the region saw a flowering in the building of hillforts and settlements of the Lusatian culture. Hillforts of the Lusatian culture, which made use of the natural conditions for protection against the enemy, are usually defended by massive ramparts. An example is the hillfort at Zemianske Podhradie from the Final Bronze Age, defended by a rampart with a timber box construction, which was built in three phases. An interesting find comes from this period – a magnificent example of a rosette brooch with stylised birds. It is a demanding product of a prehistoric craftsman, made for the splendid dress of a chieftain or another important person.

In the Late La Tène period (100 – 0 BC) the Celtic population often made use of the favourable positions of Lusatian occupation, for instance at Zemianske Podhradie, Dolná Súča, Vršatské Podhradie, Mikušovce, Krivoklát and Lednica. In the time of the occupation by the historical Celts, the area of the White Carpathians shares the Púchov culture, which alongside its native component contains elements of Celtic and, after the turn of the era, also of Roman civilisation.

After their arrival in the territory of present-day Slovakia the Slavs made use of some prehistoric upland positions, for instance at Zemianske Podhradie – the localities of Pod Hrádky, Martákova skala and Bašta – or at Horné Srnie, the locality of Ostrá hora. They were occupied again in the 9th – 10th centuries. Later settlements and stray finds from the 11th and 12th centuries at Vrbovce, Nová Bošáca and Lubina-Hrnčiarovo are evidence of the continuity of Slavic occupation after the demise of Great Moravia.

In this article we shall look at the hillfort of Martákova skala, which lies in the Bošáca valley. The first to investigate the hillfort, in the 19th century, was the Slovak researcher, scientist, botanist, polymath, folklorist, historian, archaeologist, writer, ethnographer and national awakener Jozef Ľudovít Holuby. In an article published in the journal Slovenské pohľady, volume VII of 25 October 1887, pages 217 – 221, he writes that „

below Bašta there is again Marťákova skala, the last spur of the ridge of Hradištné Vršky and Bašta to project into the Bošáca valley. Marťákova skala too (called Marťákova because near it, from ancient times, the Marťák family – still living in Zem. Podhradie today – has meadows and clearing-fields)
was enclosed from the south and the west by a triple rampart, whereas from the north and the east it is almost inaccessible and falls away steeply.
In these ramparts, which we dug through,
we found about 30 iron arrowheads
(of which we gave away more than half), a broken

point of a pike, two spurs, 5 sickles, one fine brooch (a fibula), one awl and many various pieces of iron, but no bronze at all, a number of spindle whorls of fired clay, a very large broken stag's antler,
a smaller antler sharpened at the end and one bent horn (from an ox, perhaps?). One
brass press

, the nut of which ends in an openwork Gothic ornament standing on four small columns and resembling a little lantern, which I dug up there, gives no clue now as to what it actually once served for. Here too, in the ramparts of Marťákova skala,
an abundance of coarse sherds

was dug up by us, from which the enormous dimensions of the complete vessels may be inferred. Such pots could not be used for cooking, nor did they serve as cinerary urns, but perhaps they could have been used for grain or for keeping liquids. So far we have not managed to dig up a complete pot anywhere. At Marťákova skala too it strikes everyone at once that most of the sherds and iron implements are found in the ramparts themselves, so that it seems as if those ramparts were of more recent origin, unless we are willing to allow that the houses stood on those very ramparts.“

blocks.text: In the meadow at the foot of Marťákova skala on the western side there is a hollow of which legend says that a well once stood there, into which in olden times the bells were buried, and which – so they say – can still be heard ringing in our own day at true noon. We dug this hollow out to a depth of about 2 feet and threw out of it fired clay and smaller pieces of sherds. It may be that it was a cistern, for on such dry limy ground they would hardly have cared to dig a well deep enough to reach water in sufficient quantity, when the little brook in the small valley of Rešetárovec, right below Marťákova skala, gives water enough. Further on, some 25 paces to the south-west of this hollow, there is a small hill, evidently thrown up, overgrown with oaks. Professor Könyöki and Baron Mednyanszky too, whom I brought to that four-sided hill, covering about 40 square fathoms and levelled at the top, recognised at once that it had been thrown up, of which we also convinced ourselves by digging.

children.text: Today we know that the hillfort on Martákova skala was built by the people of the Lusatian culture; the position was then occupied in the La Tène period by a Celtic population; in the Roman period the Germanic Quadi undoubtedly stayed here; and subsequently, in the Early Middle Ages – in the 9th to 11th centuries – it was inhabited by our Slavic ancestors, who left behind not only a quantity of pottery but also important metal objects, most of which, sadly, were looted in the past by metal detectorists. As will be set out below, not all of them kept their finds for themselves (or for well-funded buyers abroad), and some made it possible for archaeologists to document and publish them, which only goes to show that not all metal detectorists should be tarred with the same brush.
Besides the finds that Holuby managed to make, an interesting
Celtic hoard of iron objects

from the Late La Tène period is known from the site. The hoard was found at the foot of one of the crags of Martákova skala in 1987 and consisted of a massive iron axe with a rectangular socket, a large chisel and a knife. All three objects belong to the most common and functionally fairly universal types of tools. The axe and the chisel were used above all in felling timber, while the knife was intended mainly for domestic use or as a weapon in hunting and in combat. Analysis showed that the objects were made and buried in the Late La Tène period, probably at the turn of the last two centuries BC.
One of the interesting remains left by the Germanic Quadi living on Martákova skala is a
one-piece bronze brooch

with a four-coil spring and an upper chord. It has a regularly arched bow, ridged like a roof. Decorated in metope fashion, its foot tapers to a point and has a straight-cut heel. It is 6.7 cm long. Brooches of this type were widespread in the Late Roman period, above all in the Quadic area of south-western Slovakia. They also occur frequently in the area of the original Púchov culture. The occupation of Martákova skala by the Quadi confirms the insights historians have gained so far, namely that at a certain period the Quadi, whether for military and strategic reasons or out of necessity (as places of refuge), occupied the abandoned upland hillforts of older cultures.

That Martákova skala also belongs among the Slavic hillforts is shown, besides the pottery material, by interesting metal finds made by metal detectorists and subsequently published scientifically in the specialist literature by Dr Titus Kolník. It is an iron mount – a belt loop with a long oval loop and a rectangular fastening plate, 101 cm long. The outer arc of the loop has triple ribbing in three groups. The Slavic smith who made them used several decorative techniques here in shaping the ornamental patterns, working ingeniously with the alternation of light and shade. This belt loop demonstrates the presence of members of the ruling class at the hillfort, since it served as part of a luxurious decorative set for fastening a sword to the belt. Kolník dates the find to the first half of the 9th century – that is, to the period of the Principality of Nitra (the Blatnica–Mikulčice horizon).
Another important Slavic find – from the same metal detectorist – is a
massive iron horse bit

with straight cheekpieces. The arms of the bit are of square section, with a characteristic thickening in the middle and a break above the eye for the cheekpiece. The cheekpieces are only slightly thickened at the ends and are separated from the central part by a moulding emphasised on both sides by grooves. The maximum span of the bit is 21.3 cm. The bit belongs to type I of A. Ruttkay's typological scheme. Kolník stresses that in the case of this bit, as with several others (for example Pobedim), it is the work of a smith from the territory of present-day Slovakia and that it demonstrates the high level of the smith's craft in this territory as early as the beginning of the 9th century. Influences of Frankish art from the so-called Carolingian Renaissance also resonate in it. Originally it formed part of the equipment of a horseman, a representative of the native Slavic nobility.
These finds place Martákova skala among the
important Slavic guard hillforts

. One might consider that it fulfilled a defensive function for the Principality of Nitra against the Moravian one, and this hillfort too underlines the importance of the passes in the Lesser and the White Carpathians in the Early Middle Ages.
And in conclusion I give one legend relating to Martákova skala, which Holuby also recorded in his article.

„Legend says that Hradiská and Marťákova skala (of which there will be talk below) were inhabited by giants. Once a giant girl gathered up a ploughman with his plough and team into her apron and carried him off like a toy to the „castle“. This legend is widespread among the Germans too. That castle also had gates, and somewhere there are cellars there filled with treasures. According to another legend a town inhabited by giants stood on Hradiská, but it sank into the ground. It was so long ago, when the whole Bošáca valley as far as Bohuslavice on the Váh was still a deep lake. At all events it is remarkable that it has been preserved in the memory of the people, even if only darkly and mistily; that in ancient times a great settlement stood on Hradiská!“
